Growth Mixture Modeling

Source: R/gmm.R
fit_gmm.Rd

Fits class-specific growth curves to a continuous outcome measured repeatedly, allowing cases to vary about their own class's trajectory through random growth factors. This is the growth mixture model of Muthen & Shedden (1999) and, with random_effects = "none", latent class growth analysis for a continuous outcome.

The model is $$y_i \mid c_i = k \sim N(\Lambda (\alpha_k + \Gamma_k x_i),\; \Lambda_r \Psi_k \Lambda_r' + \Theta_k),$$ where \(\Lambda\) is the polynomial design in time, \(\alpha_k\) the growth-factor means of class \(k\), \(\Psi_k\) the covariance of the growth factors that are allowed to vary within a class, and \(\Theta_k\) the residual covariance: diagonal, the residual variances, unless residual_covariances frees some of its cells. Because the outcome is continuous the random effects integrate out in closed form, so no numerical integration is involved and the estimator is the ordinary EM algorithm the rest of the package uses.

Several outcomes. Give several outcomes measured at the same occasions (depression, anxiety and hostility at each wave, say) and each gets its own growth curve, fitted jointly: \(\Lambda\) is then one polynomial block per outcome, the classes are defined by all the curves at once, and the growth factors of every outcome share one covariance \(\Psi\), so a case's starting level on one outcome can go with its rate of change on another. This is the multivariate, or parallel-process, growth mixture model (Wickrama et al., 2022, ch. 9). The growth factors are named "<factor>_<outcome>" ("intercept_DEP", "linear_DEP", ...), and the outcomes take their names from the columns. Residuals of two outcomes measured at the same occasion usually share occasion-specific influences, which residual_covariances = "occasion" lets them carry. With several outcomes, \(\Psi\) and the residuals are held equal across classes, and growth_predictors and fix are not available yet.

A binary outcome. With family = "binomial" the outcome is 0/1 and the trajectory is a curve in its log-odds, $$\mathrm{logit}\,P(y_{it} = 1 \mid c_i = k, b_i) = \Lambda_t (\alpha_k + b_i), \qquad b_i \sim N(0, \Psi_k),$$ so cases in a class differ in where their log-odds start and how fast they change, about the class's own curve. There is no residual variance (on the logit scale it is fixed by the distribution), and the random effects no longer integrate out in closed form: the class likelihood is evaluated by Gauss-Hermite quadrature over the random effects, laid along each class's principal axes of the random effects (see n_quadrature), and maximised by EM with the random effects as missing data (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). With random_effects = "none" this is fit_lcga()(family = "binomial"), which is the model to use. The reported trajectory is the probability averaged over the random effects – the share of the class expected to answer 1 at each occasion, which is what the observed class means estimate – and fit$growth$fitted_at_mean holds the probability at the class's mean growth factors, which is lower than the average where it is above one half and higher where it is below.

A class whose cases answer exactly as its curve predicts, every one of them (all 1 early and all 0 late, say), has no finite maximum: its curve keeps steepening towards a step. Its log-odds are then held once they pass 15 in absolute value, as a response probability run to 0 or 1 is held in a latent class model, and such a class's estimates describe a near-deterministic group rather than a precise curve.

\(\Gamma_k\) is present only when growth_predictors are supplied, and is the within-class growth-factor regression: covariates shift a case's own growth factors within its class, answering "who, in this trajectory group, starts higher or grows faster?". It is a different question from predictors, which is c ON x and asks who is in the group; the two can be asked together, and are then estimated in one pass with n_steps = 1. With covariates present \(\alpha_k\) is the growth-factor intercept rather than its mean, and the reported trajectory is evaluated at the sample mean of the covariates.

Applied papers usually name a growth mixture model by what the classes are allowed to differ in, and Ram and Grimm (2009, pp. 569-570) give the three levels. Means — classes differ in mean change only — is psi = "equal", the default here. Means + Covs — classes also differ in how much interindividual variation there is within them — is psi = "free", or psi = "variances" when only the growth-factor variances differ and their covariances are held equal; the residual variances are a separate switch, residual_equal = FALSE, and should not be merged with it. Means + Covs + Pattern, where classes differ in the shape of change as well, would need class-specific time scores; fit_gmm() builds one design for every class, so that level is not available.

Two cautions worth carrying into any such analysis. Classes will be found whether or not there are groups to find: a skewed or otherwise non-normal outcome can be fitted by extra classes that are not subgroups of anyone (Jung & Wickrama, 2008, p. 305; Lee et al., 2023, p. 652, both citing Bauer & Curran, 2003). And as Ram and Grimm put it (p. 574), "groups and differences among groups will be found; but whether they represent true processes that generated the data is unknown" — the remedies they name are replication on new data and checking that class membership relates to other measured variables in the ways theory predicts.

The likelihood of a mixture of normals is unbounded: it grows without limit as a class's covariance \(\Sigma_k\) becomes singular on cases that share the same values (Kiefer & Wolfowitz, 1956; Day, 1969). An outcome with many tied scores, such as a scale with a floor, lets a class sit on the tied cases with no spread left, and a start that ends there outscores every meaningful solution while describing the ties rather than a subgroup. The search therefore counts such a start as one that did not converge and reports the best of the others (McLachlan & Peel, 2000, ch. 3); the print method says how many were set aside. A start is set aside when a class whose variances are its own – psi or the residual variances free by class – has more than 90% of itself on one value of an occasion. That is the rule every model in the package applies to its own variances, so a latent profile model, a latent transition model and a growth model call the same solution degenerate. Only when every start ends that way is such a point reported, with a warning.

Contrast fit_lcga(), which fixes the growth-factor variances at zero, so every case in a class sits on that class's curve up to occasion-level noise. LCGA is the more parsimonious model and, in criminology especially, often the preferred one; GMM is the more realistic and is what developmental psychology and epidemiology usually publish. The two are nested, so the choice can be made on BIC.

Usage

fit_gmm(
  indicator,
  n_classes = 2,
  times = NULL,
  degree = 1,
  random_effects = c("intercept_slope", "intercept", "none", "all"),
  psi = c("equal", "variances", "free"),
  residual = c("occasion", "constant"),
  residual_equal = TRUE,
  residual_covariances = NULL,
  time_scores = NULL,
  layout = c("time_major", "item_major"),
  id = NULL,
  time = NULL,
  item = NULL,
  time_labels = NULL,
  predictors = NULL,
  growth_predictors = NULL,
  growth_predictors_equal = TRUE,
  fix = NULL,
  family = c("gaussian", "binomial"),
  n_quadrature = 30,
  ...
)

Arguments

indicator

The repeated outcome. Either a wide matrix or data frame with one column per occasion, a three-dimensional array with dimensions n by 1 by times, or a long data frame together with id and time. For several outcomes (see Details), a wide matrix with one column per outcome and occasion, ordered as layout says ("time_major": every outcome at the first occasion, then every outcome at the second, ...), named like "dep_1", "anx_1", ... so the outcomes are named "dep" and "anx"; an n by outcomes by times array; or a long data frame with one column per outcome.

n_classes

Integer. Number of trajectory classes.

times

Integer. Number of occasions. Required for wide input; inferred otherwise.

degree

Degree of the polynomial in time: 1 for a linear trajectory (intercept and slope), 2 for a quadratic, and so on. Each degree needs occasions to identify it — with three time points a linear pattern can be modelled, with four a quadratic as well, and with five a cubic (Berlin et al., 2014, p. 191). Asking for more than the occasions support is an error rather than a warning.

random_effects

Which growth factors vary within a class:

  • "intercept_slope" (default) — both the intercept and the linear slope, the standard growth mixture model. Cases in a class differ both in where they start and in how fast they change.

  • "intercept" — the intercept only. Cases in a class start at different levels but change in parallel.

  • "none" — no random effects, which is latent class growth analysis; the same model as fit_lcga(family = "gaussian"), but with the residual variances free over occasions by default.

  • "all" — every growth factor, including a quadratic or higher term.

With several outcomes a keyword applies to each outcome's curve. Or name the random growth factors one by one, as c("intercept_DEP", "linear_DEP", "intercept_ANX"): a factor left out has no variance and no covariances, so every case in a class shares it, which is how a slope that does not vary is written.

psi

How the growth-factor covariance \(\Psi\) may differ across classes: held "equal" (the default); class-specific "variances" with the covariances between growth factors held equal; or estimated "free"ly in each class. "variances" sits between the other two, and with a single random effect it is the same model as "free".

\(\Psi\) is estimated without bounds. The likelihood depends on it only through each class's covariance of the repeated measures, \(\Sigma_k = \Lambda \Psi_k \Lambda' + \Theta_k\), so the maximum can lie at a \(\Psi\) with a negative variance or a correlation beyond \(\pm 1\) while every \(\Sigma_k\) remains positive definite. Such a fit is reported as estimated, with every parameter counted, and a warning names the class and the value; its log-likelihood and BIC are valid, but the value itself is not a variance or a correlation. Under "equal" or "variances" it usually means the classes' covariances differ (try "free"); under "free", that a variance is truly zero. Equality is the better default in practice as well as by convention: it is what BIC typically selects, and a class-specific \(\Psi\) is where growth mixture models most often produce a negative variance.

It is not free, though, and the cost runs the other way. Simulation work reported by Lee et al. (2023, p. 651) finds that equality restrictions on the growth-factor variances and covariances "could result in the over-extraction of latent classes and biased parameter estimates" — the within-class heterogeneity the constraint refuses to let differ between classes has to go somewhere, and an extra class is where it goes. So psi = "equal" buys stability and bounds the likelihood, and it can buy an extra class that is an artefact of the constraint. Where the number of classes is itself the finding, fit both and report which was used.

This pulls against the collapsed-variance warning, which fires more often under psi = "free". That is not a contradiction: they are the two sides of one trade-off between a model flexible enough to be realistic and one constrained enough to be estimable.

residual

Whether the residual variances are "occasion"-specific (the default) or "constant" across occasions.

residual_equal

Logical. Hold the residual variances equal across classes (the conventional default).

residual_covariances

Residual covariances to estimate, held equal across classes: NULL (the default) for none; "occasion" for every pair of outcomes measured at the same occasion; a pair of data columns, as c("DEP@T3", "DEP@T4") or "DEP@T3 with DEP@T4", for one cell, such as an outcome's residuals at two adjacent occasions; or a list of these. Columns are named "<outcome>@<occasion>", as colnames(fit$data) shows them. Needs residual = "occasion". The likelihood depends on the residual covariance only through each class's covariance of the repeated measures, which the fit keeps positive definite; if the residual covariance itself is not, a warning says so.

time_scores

Numeric values of time used in the polynomial, one per occasion. Defaults to 0, 1, ..., times - 1, which makes the intercept growth factor the level at the first occasion. Supply the actual measurement times when the occasions are unequally spaced.

layout

For wide input with a three-dimensional array or several columns per occasion, whether columns run "time_major" or "item_major".

id, time

For long input, the case and occasion identifiers, given either as column names or as vectors.

item

For long input, the column holding the outcome.

time_labels

Optional display labels for the occasions.

predictors

Optional predictors of class membership (c ON x), passed to fit_mixture()'s three-step machinery.

growth_predictors

Optional covariates regressing the growth factors themselves (i s ON x): a vector, matrix or data frame with one row per case, factors dummy-coded. These enter the measurement model rather than the structural one, so they are estimated jointly with the trajectories in a single pass regardless of n_steps. They must be complete: a case missing a covariate has no model-implied mean, and unlike a missing occasion there is nothing here to integrate it out, so remove or impute those cases first.

growth_predictors_equal

Logical. Hold the growth-factor regressions equal across classes (the conventional default). Set FALSE to let each class have its own, which asks whether a covariate matters differently in different trajectory groups.

fix

Optional data frame of growth-factor variances and covariances to hold at a given value in a given class, one row per value, with columns parameter ("growth_variance" or "growth_covariance"), item (a growth factor such as "linear", or a pair such as "intercept with linear"), class and value – the names growth_estimates() prints. Fixing every variance of one class at zero makes it a class with no variation around its own trajectory beside classes that have some (a partially constrained growth mixture); a variance fixed at zero needs its covariances fixed at zero too. Elements not fixed follow psi, so under "equal" a free element is shared by the classes where it is free. Classes are numbered by size after fitting, as always, and the fixed values move with their class; fit$growth$fix shows where they ended. Fixed values have no standard error, and blrt() refuses such a fit.

family

Distribution of the outcome given class and random effects: "gaussian" (the default) for a continuous outcome, "binomial" for a binary one in {0, 1}, modelled on the logit scale (see Details). residual, residual_equal, growth_predictors and fix apply to the continuous outcome only.

n_quadrature

family = "binomial" only: the density of the Gauss-Hermite rule over the random effects. With one random effect it is the number of nodes. With two or more, the rule is laid along each class's principal axes of the random effects, and each axis gets 2 * n_quadrature / 3 nodes per unit of the log-odds standard deviation it carries (at least n_quadrature / 10), scaled down where needed to keep within n_quadrature^q nodes for q random effects. A nearly singular growth-factor covariance, wide along one axis and narrow along the other, then gets its nodes where the likelihood needs them. The default, 30, puts the log-likelihood within about 0.003 of its limit at growth-factor variances up to 6 on the logit scale, and usually within 0.0005. Every fit is rescored at n_quadrature + 10 (fit$growth$quadrature_check), and a warning says so when the two differ by more than 0.01, which happens when a variance is much wider than that; refit with a larger n_quadrature then.

...

Further arguments passed to fit_mixture(), such as outcome and its companions, n_init, random_state, weights, strata or cluster.

Value

An object of class c("gmm", "mixture_model"). In addition to the usual fields it carries $growth, holding the design matrix, time scores, the per-class growth-factor means, the fitted class trajectories, the growth-factor covariance of each class, the residual variances and, when growth_predictors were given, $growth$coefficients: one growth-factor-by-covariate matrix per class.

References

Bock, R. D., & Aitkin, M. (1981). Marginal maximum likelihood estimation of item parameters: Application of an EM algorithm. Psychometrika, 46(4), 443-459. doi:10.1007/BF02293801

Muthen, B., & Shedden, K. (1999). Finite mixture modeling with mixture outcomes using the EM algorithm. Biometrics, 55(2), 463-469.

Berlin, K. S., Parra, G. R., & Williams, N. A. (2014). An introduction to latent variable mixture modeling (part 2): Longitudinal latent class growth analysis and growth mixture models. Journal of Pediatric Psychology, 39(2), 188-203. doi:10.1093/jpepsy/jst085

Day, N. E. (1969). Estimating the components of a mixture of normal distributions. Biometrika, 56(3), 463-474.

Kiefer, J., & Wolfowitz, J. (1956). Consistency of the maximum likelihood estimator in the presence of infinitely many incidental parameters. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 27(4), 887-906.

McLachlan, G. J., & Peel, D. (2000). Finite Mixture Models. Wiley.

Jung, T., & Wickrama, K. A. S. (2008). An introduction to latent class growth analysis and growth mixture modeling. Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 2(1), 302-317. doi:10.1111/j.1751-9004.2007.00054.x

Lee, T. K., Wickrama, K. A. S., & O'Neal, C. W. (2023). An introduction to growth mixture models (GMM). In International Encyclopedia of Education (4th ed., Vol. 14, pp. 646-655). Elsevier. doi:10.1016/B978-0-12-818630-5.10076-4

Ram, N., & Grimm, K. J. (2009). Growth mixture modeling: A method for identifying differences in longitudinal change among unobserved groups. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 33(6), 565-576. doi:10.1177/0165025409343765

Wickrama, K. A. S., Lee, T. K., O'Neal, C. W., & Lorenz, F. O. (2022). Higher-order growth curves and mixture modeling with Mplus: A practical guide (2nd ed.). Routledge. doi:10.4324/9781003158769

See also

fit_lcga() for the no-random-effects version and fit_rmlca() for trajectory classes with no growth curve at all.

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
n <- 400
cls <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
icept <- ifelse(cls == 1, 3, 1) + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
slope <- ifelse(cls == 1, 1.0, 0.2) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)
y <- outer(icept, rep(1, 4)) + outer(slope, 0:3) + matrix(rnorm(n * 4, 0, 0.7), n, 4)
fit <- fit_gmm(y, times = 4, n_classes = 2, n_init = 10, random_state = 1)
fit
